newsitem.title: BELGIUM: British bid to lift EU beef ban faces hard scrutiny.
newsitem.headline: British bid to lift EU beef ban faces hard scrutiny.

text.p: Britain's bid to take a first step in easing a worldwide ban on British beef exports faces detailed scrutiny, EU officials and diplomats said on Tuesday.

British Agriculture Minister Douglas Hogg on Tuesday wrote to EU Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler with details of a plan under which cattle from herds certified to be free of mad cow disease could be exported again after an 11-month ban.
"We will send it in accordance with the Florence agreement to the various scientific committees for examination," said Commission farm spokesman Gerard Kiely.

Kiely was referring to a deal struck at an EU summit in Florence in June 1996 setting out the steps for a gradual lifting of the crippling ban imposed the previous March when the British government admitted that a fatal brain disease, CJD, could be contracted from eating infected beef.
The EU's scientific veterinary, multi-disciplinary and other committees, made up of experts from EU member states, could be involved, Kiely said.
Asked how long this could take, Kiely said, "It's impossible to say."
In London, Hogg said in answer to a parliamentary question that he was looking for a quick EU response.

"I have urged the Commission to ensure that the consultation procedure laid down in the Florence Agreement is initiated immediately so that we can resume exports of meat from animals in export-certified herds as soon as possible," he said.
Hogg has written to fellow EU farm ministers explaining how Britain has implemented a programme to eradicate mad cow disease (bovine spongiform encephalopathy).
Britain is due next week to remove the final major obstacle to lifting the beef export ban when it starts culling an extra 100,000 cattle seen as vulnerable to BSE.
But Germany, which has taken the toughest stance on the need to protect public health against BSE, stressed the need for careful examination of the British certified herd scheme.

"We must stick to the procedures agreed in Florence that every change and new development has to be examined by the appropriate committee and a decision will be taken on the basis of scientific results," said a German official.
Other EU member states were also cautious.
"We will look at it very carefully before taking any further action," said an agricultural official from another member state.
Among the first farmers to benefit from a lifting of the ban would be those in Northern Ireland where much better records of cows' histories are kept.
